articles.title: Wisconsin dad cited after tripping 9-year-old during youth football game
articles.summary: Poor parental behavior in youth sports reached a new low near Milwaukee when a father ran onto the field and tripped a 9-year-old football player racing for the end zone, police said.
articles.body: Poor parental behavior in youth sports reached a new low near Milwaukee when a father ran onto the field and tripped a 9-year-old football player racing for the end zone, police said. Video of the incident, which quickly went viral, captured the moment Saturday at Case High School in Racine, where the Racine Youth Eagles hosted the Milwaukee Colts. An Eagles ball carrier had turned the left edge and had a clear path to the pylon when, out of nowhere, a man wearing black shorts and a black T-shirt ran onto the field, video showed. The man extended his left foot and swept the runner’s legs out from under him, causing the player to crash to the grass short of a touchdown. “During the game, a parent from the visiting team became upset over a play, walked onto the field, and tripped a 9-year-old player,” Mount Pleasant police said in a statement. “A spectator captured the incident on video, while another parent followed the suspect’s vehicle as he left the grounds. Officers located the vehicle shortly after and conducted a traffic stop,” the statement said. “The suspect, a 41-year-old Milwaukee man, admitted to the act and was issued a citation for disorderly conduct.” The Colts were awarded a touchdown on that play, and referees called the game early in hopes of defusing tensions between the victorious hosts and the defeated visitors. Terrence Ryan Bradshaw was pulled over at 11:07 a.m. Saturday on Highway 20 near Oakes Road, less than half a mile away from Case High School, Mount Pleasant police records show. Bradshaw told officers he apologized to players and coaches for losing his cool because “there was just some bigger kids (on the other team) than my kid,” according to police body camera footage of the stop. Bradshaw said he was only trying to “stop the game,” though his actions stunned officers. “I mean it’s kids. Kids!” police officer Nicole Knierim told Bradshaw. Bradshaw explained he was afraid his son might get hurt. “I got scared, really,” he told police. “My son broke his arm twice already, so when I saw him flip like that it just — I was trying to stop the game, really.” Knierim and her partner discussed the case and agreed Bradshaw deserved a disorderly conduct citation. “So there were these kids playing a game. The kids on the other team are bigger than his kids, and it was he felt it was just like getting a little too much or whatever,” Knierim said to her partner. “And he says ‘I got my feelings or whatever,’ so he didn’t kick him. He says he went out there to stop the play, and they kind of slid together. He says, ‘I apologize to everybody.’” Bradshaw does not have to appear in court if he pays the $313 fine, police said. The 9-year-old player “was thankfully not injured,” police added. Prosecutors reviewed the incident and determined it did not amount to felony child abuse, letting the disorderly conduct citation stand, the Racine County District Attorney’s Office said.

articles.title: In 2024, a Minnesota dairy began turning manure from more than 2,000 cows into renewable gas; the project can produce up to 480,000 gasoline-gallon equivalents a year
articles.summary: US News: On a 55-acre dairy farm in rural Minnesota, manure from more than 2,000 milking cows is being turned into ultra-low-carbon vehicle fuel that is sent d.
articles.body: On a 55-acre dairy farm in rural Minnesota, manure from more than 2,000 milking cows is being turned into ultra-low-carbon vehicle fuel that is sent directly into interstate natural gas pipelines. The renewable natural gas (RNG) facility at Ash Grove Dairy near Lake Benton processes up to 60,000 gallons of cow manure every day. Built by Dynamic Renewables and funded through a $22 million joint venture led by Clean Energy Fuels Corp, the plant converts farm waste into clean biomethane for commercial transportation fleets across North America. At full capacity, the Minnesota facility is expected to produce around 480,000 gasoline-gallon equivalents of negative carbon-intensity fuel every year. The project was showed in industry reports by Biofuels Digest and Farm Progress after Clean Energy Fuels announced that the facility had officially connected to the national pipeline network.Turning cow manure into pipeline fuelLarge dairy farms produce huge amounts of organic waste, which naturally releases methane as it breaks down in manure storage ponds. Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas that has a much stronger warming effect than carbon dioxide over shorter periods. At Ash Grove Dairy, manure is collected throughout the day and pumped into large sealed anaerobic digesters. Inside these oxygen-free tanks, microorganisms break down the organic material while capturing methane gas before it escapes into the atmosphere. The captured biogas is then sent through cleaning and upgrading equipment at the site. The system removes water, hydrogen sulphide, carbon dioxide and other impurities, producing biomethane that has the same chemical properties as conventional natural gas. The cleaned gas is pressurised and injected into the commercial pipeline system. From there, Clean Energy Fuels delivers it through its nationwide network of refuelling stations used by transit buses, municipal garbage trucks and long-haul freight vehicles.Expanding cleaner fuel for transportThe Ash Grove project is the fifth renewable natural gas facility opened by Clean Energy Fuels within nine months, showing the growing demand for lower-emission fuel across agriculture and commercial transportation. Heavy-duty vehicles produce a significant share of transport-related emissions. As federal and state climate rules become stricter, many fleet operators are moving away from traditional diesel engines and adopting compressed natural gas and biomethane-powered vehicles. "Ash Grove is our fifth renewable natural gas facility to come online in the last nine months," Clay Corbus, senior vice president at Clean Energy Fuels, said in the company's official announcement. "With the growing demand for RNG, and interest really starting to take off as fleets realize how effective and immediate they can fuel cleanly, the RNG produced at Ash Grove will directly help with reducing carbon emissions across the country." Because anaerobic digesters stop methane from dairy manure from being released directly into the atmosphere, fuel produced from cow waste receives a negative carbon intensity score under lifecycle environmental standards, including California's Low Carbon Fuel Standard.Benefits for dairy farmers and the environmentFor dairy farms such as Ash Grove, anaerobic digestion provides benefits beyond reducing greenhouse gas emissions. After the manure completes the digestion process, the remaining material, called digestate, is separated into solid and liquid portions. The solid material can be reused as nutrient-rich animal bedding or processed into a soil conditioner, while the liquid portion is applied to farm fields as a more stable, lower-odour fertiliser. Farm Progress reports that turning manure into a renewable energy product gives family-owned dairy farms another source of income while also improving how nutrients are managed on agricultural land. Agriculture produces about 10 per cent of all greenhouse gas emissions in the United States, with livestock manure management contributing a noticeable share of that total. By capturing methane directly from farm waste, dairy producers and energy companies can transform an environmental challenge into a valuable source of cleaner transportation fuel.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: National Testing Agency gets three senior officers amid exam overhaul
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Centre has brought in three senior officers, including an IPS officer, at the National Testing Agency (NTA), giving the embattled exami.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Centre has brought in three senior officers, including an IPS officer, at the National Testing Agency (NTA), giving the embattled examination body fresh administrative muscle as it undergoes one of its biggest personnel and security overhauls following controversies over NEET-UG and UGC-NET.IPS officer Ravi Kumar Singh and IAS officer Prasanna Venkatesh V have been appointed directors at NTA, while Amit Samdariya, a 2016-batch Indian Revenue Service (customs and indirect taxes) officer, will join as joint director. The appointments were cleared through separate personnel ministry orders dated August 27.The induction comes days after NTA began a wider revamp that includes removing around 600 experts from its examination panels, onboarding a fresh set of specialists and introducing a four-tier scrutiny mechanism for question papers. The agency is also strengthening examination security, recruiting additional officials and moving to new premises where security is proposed to be reinforced with CISF deployment. The measures were reviewed recently by Union education minister Pralhad Joshi as the govt sought to tighten both the academic and operational ends of the examination process.NTA has been under sustained pressure since the NEET-UG paper leak controversy, which triggered nationwide protests and intensified scrutiny of how high-stakes examinations are secured and administered.More recently, it was forced to order fresh UGC-NET examinations in english, commerce and sociology after multiple errors and repeated questions were detected in the June papers, adding a question-paper quality problem to its security challenges.The personnel ministry has directed all three officers to take charge within three weeks.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Sonia memoir row deepens, Congress alleges government pressure
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: A controversy has erupted over the Indian publication of Sonia Gandhi's memoir 'Belonging', with Penguin Random House India (PRHI) reported.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A controversy has erupted over the Indian publication of Sonia Gandhi's memoir 'Belonging', with Penguin Random House India (PRHI) reportedly pulling out of the deal following differences with the former Congress president over certain suggested edits.Calling it a "murder of democracy", Congress functionary Ashok Gehlot alleged that "pressure was put on Penguin India to remove the portions related to Narendra Modi, RSS and China's occupation of Indian territory during Modi's rule".Penguin, for its part, issued a carefully worded statement saying: "PRHI is not the publisher of 'Belonging' in India. Any suggestion that PRHI decided not to publish it because the author declined editorial changes does not accurately reflect the circumstances." The publishing house, however, defended its "prerogative and responsibility" to fact-check manuscripts and make recommendations to authors. It also said it remained "willing and keen" to publish the book. Earlier this year, PRHI stopped the distribution of cartoonist Joe Sacco's 'The Once and Future Riot', on the Muzaffarnagar riots.Interestingly, the US publisher of the memoir, Alfred A Knopf, is also a division of Penguin Random House. The international launch of ‘Belonging: A Journey in Love’, featuring a photo of a young Sonia on its cover, is scheduled for Nov 10. There is a question mark over who the Indian rights of ‘Belonging’ belong to, but the buzz is that HarperCollins may bag them.Gehlot also questioned why PRHI wanted changes to the Indian edition if Knopf was ready to publish the book worldwide in its original form. “What is the reason or what pressure is there that what is being published across the world cannot be published in India?” he asked. “Why is this truth being hidden from the people of India? Will the Modi govt alter even the facts by pressuring publishers?” he added.Gehlot said the integrity and dignity with which Sonia had served the country were exemplary. “Suppressing the book of a person of such stature, a senior leader of the nation, and former leader of the opposition, is tantamount to the murder of freedom of expression,” he said.Deputy leader of the opposition in Lok Sabha Gaurav Gogoi said, “No doubt there are those in the BJP govt who have now become afraid of a book being read by the people of India.”Congress, from its official social media handle to frontal organisations such as Seva Dal, lashed out at what it called the BJP’s attempt to sabotage the book of a senior national figure.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Forced birth control in Greenland violated women’s rights, experts find
articles.summary: Truth commission to be established after two expert reports failed to agree whether scheme constituted genocide.
articles.body:
Greenland is establishing a truth and reconciliation commission surrounding a decades-long forced contraceptive scheme against Indigenous girls and women, after two expert reports failed to agree whether it constituted genocide.

From the 1960s to the 1990s, at least 4,000 Greenlandic Inuits – including girls as young as 12 – received intrauterine devices (IUDs) or contraceptive injections, often without their consent or knowledge, a joint Danish-Greenlandic inquiry found last year.

That inquiry found the practice was intended to reduce birth rates and family sizes, which Danish authorities at the time viewed as a way to improve living standards and social and health conditions in Greenland, an Arctic island and semi-sovereign territory of Denmark, with a population of 57,000.

Greenland’s government tasked a four-member commission in 2024 with investigating the campaign, which led some victims to suffer serious infections, scarring of the fallopian tubes or removal of the uterus. Some were later unable to have children.

But the experts could not reach a unanimous conclusion, Greenland’s Justice Minister Marianne Paviasen told reporters on Friday, with one report stating there was no genocide and the other saying the extent of the violations could not be established.

“We cannot say, on behalf of the government, whether there was genocide. This is something we can continue to debate,” Paviasen said.

Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the reconciliation commission would “not be about assigning blame, but about uncovering the truth with a view to genuine reconciliation”.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Copenhagen would “handle the political process together with the government of Greenland”.

The Greenlandic Siumut Party, however, urged the genocide question to be settled by “a competent and independent international court”.

“Today we could have been far more Greenlanders,” the party added.

Victims have questioned why no Greenlandic Inuit were appointed as experts while recounting painful histories dug up by the panel.

“For me, this is not just about history or politics. It’s my body, my life, and my right to self-determination,” Henriette Berthelsen told the AFP news agency.

“And once again, I see that it is others who will investigate and define what was done to me and to other Inuit women,” she added.

Inger Platou, 70, told Reuters she had woken up from what she had been told was a minor operation only to discover an IUD had been inserted without her consent.

“It turns out we were treated like animals,” she said. “Without consent, they just wanted to stop women from giving birth or having children. It was a very inhumane act.”

Complications from the coil left her unable to become pregnant, she said.

Denmark apologised for the scheme last year, with Frederiksen describing “systematic discrimination” against Greenlanders.

On Thursday, the Danish parliament agreed that women affected by the forced contraception campaign can claim compensation of up to 300,000 Danish crowns ($46,758) each.

articles.title: Clean energy push unfair on developing nations: CJI Surya Kant
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: CJI Surya Kant on Friday told Commonwealth Countries that it is unfair that the industrialised countries, who took two centuries to adopt c.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: CJI Surya Kant on Friday told Commonwealth Countries that it is unfair that the industrialised countries, who took two centuries to adopt clean energy, are asking the nations in the process of industrialisation to move towards renewable energy within decades.Speaking at the Commonwealth Secretariat in London, CJI Kant said, “Countries that are finally industrialising are being asked to move rapidly towards renewable power, and often made to bear the brunt of criticism when they cannot move fast enough. In comparison, the nations urging that transition spent two centuries building their own strength on coal and oil,” he said.Addressing the common platform for 56 countries on “Policy dialogue on climate justice”, the CJI said the cumulative shift of commonwealth countries to clean energy depends on copper, cobalt and lithium, extraction of which carries environmental and social consequences.Developing countries facing myriad challenges depending on their geographical locations and pushing them towards clean energy at an unrealistic pace could create more challenges than solutions, he warned.Justice Kant said, “The challenge, therefore, is to reconcile the urgency of the clean energy transition with the principles of fairness and shared responsibility that must underpin it.”He said the Supreme Court of India and the HCs have played a significant role in protecting the environment, ecology and its endangered species. He recounted the Zambian HC making a copper mining company liable for polluting water. Commonwealth countries can learn from each other’s experience to bolster efforts towards smoother transition towards clean energy without making their populations pay a heavy price, he said.“We need not develop a separate jurisprudential vocabulary in every country where a climate question reaches the Courts. Rather, the Courts should be open to borrowing ideas, approaches, and solutions that have proved useful elsewhere in the Commonwealth, while adapting them carefully to their own constitutional, social, and environmental circumstances,” he said.“Courts must be willing to search for solutions that protect the environment without losing sight of the legitimate needs of development, and to recognise that the two need not always be cast as choices in which one must defeat the other,” CJI Kant said.He cited the case before SC where the officials were accused of felling many trees to widen a road for access to a super specialty hospital for wounded para-military forces. “We had no wish to reward officials who had cut trees; equally, we had no wish to deny wounded soldiers an ambulance route,” he said.Instead of halting the widening of roads, the SC had ordered extensive compensatory afforestation. “We still monitoring that afforestation today… development and preservation do not always have to stand on opposite sides of the scales. Sometimes, the task of a Court is to find the third way to promote both routes through judicial creativity,” he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Junk foods will soon have labels warning of high salt, sugar and fat
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Junk foods will soon carry warning labels highlighting high levels of salt, sugar and fat, with the Food Safety and Standards Authority of .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Junk foods will soon carry warning labels highlighting high levels of salt, sugar and fat, with the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) telling Supreme Court on Friday that it has agreed to red-coloured hexagonal warnings on the front of food packages to help consumers identify products high in specified nutrients of concern.FSSAI conveyed its position through a compliance affidavit filed before Supreme Court in response to the court's Aug 13 order on front-of-pack labelling (FoPL).The move comes after the court pushed Centre to act on the issue, saying, "If the Union does it on its own, well and good, otherwise we shall proceed to pass further directions."Under the framework, products high in specified nutrients would carry prominent red hexagonal warnings reading "HIGH FAT", "HIGH SALT" and/or "HIGH SUGAR", as applicable.FSSAI has agreed to exempt single-ingredient foods such as ghee, edible oil, salt, sugar, jaggery and honey from the proposed warnings, subject to applicable food safety and labelling regulations.The regulator has agreed to implement FoPL in phases, giving the industry time to reformulate products. Phase I would cover products high in two or more specified nutrients, while Phase II would extend warnings to products high in any one specified nutrient.The framework is based on nutrient thresholds specified under the Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024, issued by ICMR-NIN. The affidavit follows the Supreme Court’s observations on public health, particularly amid concerns over the rising prevalence of childhood obesity. The court said front-of-pack labelling could help consumers make informed purchasing decisions.The case stems from a PIL filed by NGO 3S and Our Health Society, which approached Supreme Court through advocate Rajiv Shankar Dwivedi, seeking front-of-pack labelling to help consumers make informed choices.FSSAI said the system is intended to provide a “simple, prominent and easily comprehensible warning” to consumers about food products high in specified nutrients of concern. It also cited international examples, including Chile and Canada, where front-of-pack labelling has been adopted.Supreme Court had considered options including coloured indicators, interpretative words, numbers, letters, symbols and percentages for front-of-pack labelling and directed Centre to take a decision and place it on record.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Government tightens norms for e-cycles, e-bikes
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI:  The road transport ministry has proposed to tighten technical and safety norms for low-speed electric cycles and e-bikes with a maximum sp.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The road transport ministry has proposed to tighten technical and safety norms for low-speed electric cycles and e-bikes with a maximum speed of 25 kmph and motor power below 600 watts. Manufacturers of these would have to get vehicles certified by authorised testing agencies before they can qualify for exemption from the Motor Vehicles Act to be treated as “motor vehicle”.At present, electric two-wheelers that have motor power below 250 watts are not treated as “motor vehicles” and hence don’t need registration. This definition is now being expanded to vehicles that have motor power up to 600 watts, which officials said is “realistic”.All these vehicles will be required to use only lithium-ion batteries instead of lead-acid batteries.As per draft amendments to Central Motor Vehicles Rules, such vehicles will have to be fitted with “suitable brakes and retro-reflective devices” for visibility. The draft notification said for pedal-assisted electric bicycles, the motor assistance must progressively reduce and cut off once the vehicle reaches 25 kmph or when the rider stops pedalling.The proposal is significant considering that low-speed electric two-wheelers have witnessed rapid growth as affordable urban mobility options, but many models have operated with limited regulatory oversight.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Brazil’s TV and radio campaign blitz begins, with Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro set for a nasty fight
articles.summary: RIO DE JANEIRO — Brazil’s top presidential candidates, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro, beginning Friday will seek to draw votes through free advertisements on television and radio stations, which continue to play a fundamental role in the campaign despite the rise of social media, experts say.
articles.body: RIO DE JANEIRO — Brazil’s top presidential candidates, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro, beginning Friday will seek to draw votes through free advertisements on television and radio stations, which continue to play a fundamental role in the campaign despite the rise of social media, experts say. Even in a heavily online country such as Brazil, ads on the TV and radio continue to set the talk of the town and sway voters, reaching remote corners of the continental-sized country. With the incumbent Lula — who is seeking a fourth, nonconsecutive term — currently polling neck and neck with Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, his main rival and the eldest son of ex-President Jair Bolsonaro, independent political consultant and former Brazilian minister Thomas Traumann expects the ads to be extremely belligerent. “I think the campaign will be dirtier than 2022, and 2022 was already one of the dirtiest in Brazilian history,” Traumann said, referencing the last presidential election when Lula defeated former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is currently serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup, by the thinnest margin since Brazil’s return to democracy in 1985. Much like ubiquitous Brazil flags and elaborate street paintings signal World Cup season, campaign ads on the television and radio indicate upcoming elections and put the contest at the forefront of Brazilians’ minds. Maria Izabel Pecanha, an 84-year-old retired history teacher from Rio de Janeiro, says many voters like her will not pay attention to ads on social media and will instead watch those on the radio and TV as she has done since the 1950s. “I like to watch them to feel excited, to feel angry, to think of how Brazil’s political actors show themselves. It is always very instructive,” Pecanha said by phone. “I have watched today’s and I will keep doing that until the end of the campaign, it is like watching a bit of history unfold.” Unlike in the U.S., Brazilian campaign ads are free of cost to parties, and airtime is distributed according to the size of the coalition and representation in the lower house. The gratuity of ads “defends the democratic principle of equal treatment and means the amount of time each party gets is not going to be determined by the economic power of each party,” said Bruno Pompeu, a communications and advertising professor at the University of Sao Paulo. Over the years, the tone, style and nature of these spots have evolved. The rise of social media and its more casual language will likely influence campaign ads on the more traditional platforms, said João Ricardo Matta, a business professor at the Getulio Vargas Foundation, a think-tank and university. “They will be less artificial, more natural, with the appearance of something homemade,” said Matta, who also expects funds that were traditionally allocated to the production of TV and radio ads to shift to campaign material on social media. Ahead of the first round of voting on Oct. 4, broadcasters must reserve 14 minutes a day for nearly 1,000 30-second ads, in addition to blocks lasting 12 minutes and 30 seconds exclusively for presidential candidates. Of those blocks, Lula and allied parties will get 5 minutes and 31 seconds, while Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro’s party will get 4 minutes and 20 seconds. The remaining time will be divided between two other parties. That Flávio Bolsonaro will get less time than Lula illustrates that he has struggled to unite major parties behind his candidacy, said Traumann, unlike his father who won in 2018. In the case of a run-off vote, slated for Oct. 25, the two remaining candidates will get an equal amount of time.

articles.title: Ebola spreads to two new zones in DRC; 60 areas now affected
articles.summary: DRC’s is the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak ever recorded, with 5,794 confirmed cases and 2,786 deaths.
articles.body:
The fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak in history has reached two new health zones in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), with a total of 60 areas now affected, according to the latest government figures.

The two new zones affected are Biena and Manguredjipa in DRC’s North Kivu province, where the fatality rate is much higher than the overall rate of 48 percent, partly due to delayed response efforts, according to data by the Ministry of Health released on Friday.

The ministry said the outbreak in DRC has recorded 5,794 confirmed cases, including 2,786 deaths, and is spreading at an unprecedented speed – faster than efforts to track and slow it.

Efforts to contain the outbreak have been hampered by armed conflict in the affected provinces, displacement, attacks on medical personnel and facilities, a mobile working population, and a lack of critical infrastructure.

The outbreak is now on track to surpass the deadliest Ebola epidemic on record – the 2014 to 2016 outbreak in West Africa that killed more than 11,000 people.

Meanwhile, aid group Doctors Without Borders – known by its French acronym MSF – said on Friday it had opened a new treatment centre in Beni in North Kivu in the country’s northeast to enable a faster response in what it said was one of the hardest-hit areas.

Beni has recorded 122 confirmed cases and 87 deaths since the start of the outbreak in mid-May, with an Ebola fatality rate of close to 69 percent, one of the highest in the country, according to the latest government figures.

Aid workers have said that a shortage of bed capacity is one of the factors hampering the response to the outbreak. The new centre “enables the rapid treatment of patients, strengthens contact tracing and supports the health authorities in their efforts to contain the spread of the virus,” MSF said in a statement.

There is no approved vaccine or treatment for this particular strain of Ebola, known as Bundibugyo , which is rarer than the virus type behind most past outbreaks. This means that relief workers are more reliant on traditional methods like tracing contacts and ⁠isolating patients to try to control ⁠its spread.

MSF currently has 1,400 staff in DRC supporting the response, ‌and operates ‌treatment centres with a total of 400 beds.

“Early diagnosis and treatment as soon as the first symptoms appear significantly increase people’s chances of survival, whilst reducing the risk of transmission ‌ within families and communities,” MSF emergency coordinator Albert Stern said.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned on Thursday that Ebola is spreading faster than efforts to contain it.

“The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is the fastest-spreading Ebola epidemic ever recorded,” he said in a post on US social media company X. “It’s growing faster and wider than the response to contain it.

“We know how to contain Ebola and save lives. The world must urgently step up action to get it under control.”

articles.title: Business' relief as Edinburgh's Princes Street finally reopens
articles.summary: A large section of the street has been closed through festival season after a devastating fire.
articles.body:
Edinburgh's Princes Street is set to fully reopen on Saturday, seven weeks after it was shut by a major fire in a former department store.

Businesses in the east of the city say they have taken a hit during the usually-lucrative festival season, as disruption to public transport has hit footfall.

Bus routes have been diverted and tram services have only been operating in the west of the city while work to make the building safe took place.

Edinburgh council leader Jane Meagher said she was delighted the thoroughfare was reopening but acknowledged it had been a difficult chapter for the city.

The Scottish government previously committed £5m to the recovery effort , allowing some businesses to offset lost revenue.

The fire happened on 9 July, with Princes Street's reopening coming two days before the last day of the Edinburgh Festival Fringe on Monday.

Alistair Brown – founder of Bellfield Brewery, which runs Nobles on Constitution Street – said regular tram services meant the prospect of new customers every seven minutes.

Despite being optimistic about the return of the trams, Brown said it was too early to assess the full financial damage to his business.

He told BBC Scotland News: "I am relieved but still apprehensive. We have lost a lot of business through no fault of our own and it will take time to see how we recover from this.

"This is our busiest time of year that gets us through the quieter months from January to March but because of the disruption we have been quieter than March.

"So we will have to wait until next year to see the full impact.

"I never thought I'd be so excited to hear the ding of a tram. It just shows you don't fully appreciate things till they are gone."

Adam Barclay, manager of Argonaut Books, said businesses should be able to expect better from elected representatives after a month of "radio silence" from City of Edinburgh Council.

He said: "In what is surely some sort of cosmic joke, the trams will be up and running again just in time for the Fringe to be over - we missed the whole thing.

"The residents and businesses of Leith have been dealing with 20 minute plus delays on buses, massively reduced footfall and a council effectively asleep at the wheel.

"It has undoubtedly had a profound negative impact on our trading this summer and it will have knock-on effects far beyond this one month.

"In what should have been our busiest non-December period, we performed worse than an average month - this is factoring in 16 sold-out book Fringe events."

Chef Dean Banks runs restaurants across the city in the west end and on Constitution Street.

Banks said there was a drop in takings at all the restaurants due to the street closure and diversions.

"We are obviously delighted that the trams will be up and running again," he said. "It will bring business back down to Leith but to the city centre as well.

"What we found during the Fringe was that our city centre venues were impacted as well because members of the public were avoiding Princes Street and the west end.

"But in Leith we saw a huge decrease over the Fringe, the revenues were about 50% down."

The Masterchef star said the council could have done more as it was one of the busiest times of year for the city.

"It is great Princes Street is opening now but it does feel like it is a little bit too little too late for this time of year," he said.

"It could have been sorted out. I am disappointed with the communication with Edinburgh council and the way they handled it.

"They were given millions of pounds from the government.

"They could easily have moved those trams and helped the city flourish during its Fringe which puts Edinburgh on the world stage in August," he said.

As Princes Street reopens to all traffic, a section of the pavement directly outside the burnt-out building will remain closed while work continues.

Pedestrians will be partially diverted on to the eastbound road, which will be reduced to one lane at that section.

Three bus stops between Castle Street and Frederick Street will also remain closed to reduce congestion, but bus services will run along Princes Street, rather than the current diversion along George Street.

Jane Meagher acknowledged it had been an incredibly difficult chapter, particularly for businesses on the northern end of the tram line.

She said the council had worked closely with Lothian Buses and Edinburgh Trams to limit disruption.

She added that it had worked closely with partners to communicate how the fire affected the city through dedicated online channels.

"This period has further underlined the critical importance and popularity of our tram network, not just to the north of the city but to the whole of Edinburgh," she said.

"Whilst their return will be most welcome, we need to consider how we can properly safeguard this vital service to meet the needs and challenges of our growing city."

A campaign for businesses in Leith and Newhaven will also be rolled out through the coming months and into the winter festive period to provide support.

Council officers have been out visiting premises in the area to explain how the More by the Shore campaign will work and listen to feedback.

articles.title: 'A huge vanity project' - when Sputnik crash-landed in Scotland
articles.summary: Ten years after Sputnik News opened in Edinburgh, why did Scotland become a front in the global disinformation war?
articles.body:
Ten years ago, an alien object entered Scotland's airspace for the first time.

The website and internet radio station Sputnik News was named after the first man-made satellite which was launched into space in 1957.

The size of a basketball, the original Sputnik emitted a simple beep for three weeks before its battery died.

But the signal it sent the world's governments was much more significant. It showed that the Soviet Union was winning the space race, and that news jolted the west into action.

Almost 60 years later, its namesake was met with similar alarm.

Sputnik News is not like other media organisations. Wholly owned by the Russian government, it's widely recognised as a propaganda tool for President Vladimir Putin.

And in August 2016 it brought a new era of state-sponsored disinformation to Britain at a crucial time in its recent history.

How Russia is quietly trying to win over the world beyond the West

Sputnik's Edinburgh operation lasted barely five years, and throughout that time faced accusations of stoking conspiracy theories to destabilise the UK.

A decade on, it's tempting to look back on its time in Scotland as a weird blip or just another failed media enterprise.

But that would be a mistake, according to former SNP MP Stewart McDonald.

"We are a society ripe for hostile disinformation," he says. "We're deeply divided, we're polarised politically, we're polarised socially. We struggle economically.

"That's perfect for hostile disinformation operations. And that's what Russian state media does.

The Scotland in which Sputnik landed in 2016 was going through a turbulent time. In the wake of the 2014 referendum , a wave of new media enterprises were making the case for independence.

Established online outlets Wings over Scotland and Bella Caledonia were joined by digital news platforms CommonSpace and Broadcasting Scotland.

Subscription and supporter-led services, they offered an alternative to what was increasingly becoming known as the "mainstream media" - specifically corporate-owned newspapers, commercial broadcasters, and the BBC.

Carolyn Scott was one of the many young activist-journalists drawn to this new media landscape.

A folk singer and musician, she'd become increasingly politically active during the referendum, alongside a friend from the traditional music scene, Jack Foster. The pair ran a folk music podcast for a few years but had never managed to make money from it.

Then, according to Carolyn: "The day after the referendum, Jack contacted me about setting up a new media company and we got some crowdfunding to kind of see what was feasible. We did that for a year.

"We launched a weekly podcast that turned into four or five weekly podcasts and then some kind of YouTube TV stuff as well... but the whole time we had like zero income."

They had an audience, but not enough to make a living, and so towards the end of 2015 they were forced to wrap up the company

A few months later Carolyn learned Sputnik News was coming to Edinburgh and was advertising for journalists.

The Russian state-owned news agency Rossiya Segodnya set up Sputnik in November 2014 as a sister service to RT – formerly Russia Today – the Kremlin's global television news service. Both broadcast the Putin government's view of foreign affairs around the world.

Dr Ammon Cheskin is an expert on Russian politics at the University of Glasgow. He sees the Sputnik of 2016 as part of a strategy of projecting Russian might.

"It looked like the sort of thing a great power would do," he says.

"In the same way that the UK might have the BBC, they would have this network of journalists. I think it was a kind of a facade of great power status.

"Anybody that studies Russian foreign policy knows that one of the key priorities has been to prove that Russia is actually a great power on par with all the other great powers in the world."

Carolyn Scott was aware there were questions around Sputnik's editorial independence but believes the more established RT was not then seen as beyond the pale.

"Throughout 2014 and 2015, RT had managed to get itself into a place where it had an OK reputation, a fairly decent reputation in a lot of the circles that we were kind of active in," she says.

"There were a lot of political commentators from across Scotland and the UK hosting their own shows on RT. And it was very much billed to us as it's just a radio version of that."

"I certainly didn't go into the job singing and dancing and thinking: 'This is amazing, this is spectacular, it's going to be brilliant'," she says.

"It was: 'I need to pay my bills, and this is going to help wipe out some debt'. And we were going to have pretty much editorial freedom to just run our own show."

Sputnik launched from Edinburgh in August 2016 and the response from the native media was sceptical, even hostile. It was immediately suspected of coming to Scotland to create and amplify tensions within the UK.

The Daily Record dubbed it "Radio Gaga" and accused it of running stories that the independence referendum had been rigged.

The Herald called it "Putin's Sputnik" and an editorial in The Times said: "Those Nationalists who welcome the arrival of Sputnik are ignoring the Russian leader's record as an autocratic ruler."

Carolyn had signed up to co-present a daily radio programme. Immediately, she felt there were problems.

"It was an absolute chaotic mess. The idea that Sputnik could influence any election or referendum in this country was laughable. They wouldn't even influence a local dog show," she says.

"They had no idea what they were doing. The staff base was completely inexperienced. There was a woman who was basically brought in as an executive producer. Her background was that she was a hotel receptionist."

Nevertheless, Sputnik was seen as relentlessly anti-Nato, pro-Russian, and pro-Donald Trump. Later, it would be accused of peddling conspiracy theories about the Covid pandemic and the war in Ukraine.

It's important to remember the context in which Sputnik was operating in 2016.

The UK had just voted to leave the European Union and David Cameron had stood down as prime minister, to be replaced by Theresa May.

Brexit dominated UK politics, and in Scotland that, in turn, contributed to the SNP dominating the 2015 and 2016 Westminster and Holyrood elections.

Despite losing the 2014 referendum, the pro-independence movement appeared to be on the front foot.

Sputnik made much of the pro-indy credentials of its leading journalists. Looking back, Carolyn believes that was always the strategy.

"I realise now that I think their entire point was let these slightly left-wing progressive types do the show that they want," she says.

"They gave us free rein because that might build some legitimacy so that one day, when they've got an audience, they can just flip to their own agenda.

"And I see now in hindsight, that's kind of what I think their aim perhaps was."

Stewart McDonald was one of 56 SNP MPs elected in 2015 . He would become his party's defence spokesman, and one of Sputnik's most high-profile critics.

From quite early on, he wanted to put "clear blue water" between it and the SNP.

"We very deliberately set about making RT and Sputnik as toxic as possible," he says.

"People knew that going on it, I would openly criticise them.

"I think that's partly why so few people did go on it, because they understood this is not a good thing for us to be seen to be engaging with."

But some were happy to get involved with the Russian outlets.

In 2017, former First Minister Alex Salmond was condemned for hosting a talk show on RT, denounced by one opponent as "Putin's puppet". His successor, Nicola Sturgeon, said: "His choice of channel would not have been my choice."

A year later, the former SSP MSP Tommy Sheridan began presenting and writing for Sputnik.

By then, Carolyn Scott and Jack Foster were long gone. They bailed in the spring of 2017 in the face, she says, of increasingly unacceptable editorial pressure.

But speaking to the BBC in 2018, Sputnik's UK editor Nikolai Gorshkov denied the company had an agenda.

"We're not trying to influence Scottish thinking, because being based in Edinburgh, we do now realise how fiercely independently minded the Scots are," he said.

The poisoning of former double agent Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia in Salisbury in 2018, followed by allegations of Russian interference in the following year's UK election, saw relations between the two countries collapse.

That tension put Sputnik at the heart of the disinformation war, though not for long.

The company announced the closure of its UK operation in 2021, describing the move as part of a plan to reorganise its international presence more effectively.

The following year, Russia's invasion of Ukraine made it an international pariah. Nations across the world imposed economic and cultural sanctions.

In March 2022, the regulator Ofcom revoked RT's UK broadcasting licence and the European Union banned Sputnik and RT over their coverage of the war. Both services remain banned on many social media apps and websites.

Today, Sputnik's website says it continues to operate out of 17 countries in Africa, Asia and the Americas.

Putin's war in Ukraine marked the end of Russia's period of soft power, according to Ammon Cheskin.

"The whole network of it was just a huge vanity project that was ineffective. It cost lots of money and didn't reach many people, but it kind of looked good for those people that wanted to claim that Russia was a great power," he says.

"I preferred it to what came afterwards. It just highlighted the limits of Russian influence. Russia thought it could influence people and states through these mechanisms and it clearly couldn't.

"And it therefore moved to a different phase, which was much more aggressive, and militaristic. And that's where Russia's true influence was."

Stewart McDonald views Russia's disinformation programme as one part of a wider war that now sees drones flown over European airports, attacks on sub-sea cables , and cyber-hacks on institutions.

"The warning at the end is you've got to take any kind of foreign disinformation seriously," he says.

"This is a problem and a threat that is getting more sophisticated at a rate that we're just not at all keeping up with.

"You think about what that means in peacetime, but what does it mean in a time of crisis? Like a pandemic, or a kinetic war, or when your sub-sea cables get cut, or if there's a cyber-attack on Network Rail that brings the central belt to a halt.

"Or during an election campaign. Have governments even thought about how they deal with that sort of thing? No, they haven't."

Post-Sputnik, Carolyn Scott has built a new career teaching journalism at Edinburgh Napier University. She finds talking about that time painful but understands the criticism she and her colleagues faced.

"I think if you've got a foreign government launching a media company in your country that's got quite a controversial past, then it's fair game that the media is going to have a go," she says.

"I do feel physically sick talking today about it. I make sure to tell my students that we learn from our mistakes, and we take ownership of them, we don't shy away from them.

"But it's hard not to see it as one of the stupidest things I've ever done in my life. It is one of the biggest regrets I have."

articles.title: Tibet-Nepal floods: Shocking footage isn't being shown in China - and we know little about victims there
articles.summary: Some of the most dramatic footage from the deadly flash flooding is hidden from public view in China.
articles.body:
The dramatic footage was almost impossible to miss. A torrent of water tearing through Gyirong Port, one of the main border crossings between Nepal and Tibet, sweeping away all in its path as hundreds of people fled for their lives.

The scenes, captured by CCTV cameras, quickly spread on social media and onto screens around the world.

Only a single still-frame shot has been broadcast so far by the country's state-run flagship news bulletin.

It has also been difficult to find the video on China's heavily censored internet. It is just as hard to even find posts describing the flash flooding that has claimed hundreds of lives, with just as many still unaccounted for since Wednesday.

Beijing has launched a massive rescue operation involving hundreds of emergency workers, which is continuing, and President Xi Jinping chaired an emergency meeting with officials to co-ordinate efforts.

But when you compare the country's internet content to what much of the world has been seeing online these past few days, China's firewall becomes more visible than ever.

Tibet, which Beijing annexed in the 1950s, had long resisted rule by the Chinese Communist Party.

China has quashed protests over the years, sometimes violently, and has been accused of grave rights violations in the Buddhist region. It has labelled the exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, a separatist.

That history means the very name Tibet draws China's censors. Beijing's sensitivities are especially apparent at times likes this.

There have been daily updates on the missing and the dead, and Beijing has also been posting updates on the rescue operations, as well as the dangers posed by a barrier lake that has been at risk of overflowing.

But there is little detail beyond that. There are no accounts from survivors in Tibet, and almost no user-generated footage showing the deadly moments or their aftermath.

We are yet to hear from anxious families of those missing. Trying to contact people there is near-impossible during regular times.

As a journalist who has covered North Korea, it has often been easier for me to contact interviewees in Pyongyang than it is in the Tibetan capital, Lhasa.

On Thursday night, as global headlines led on the devastation in a Himalayan valley, China's state broadcaster opened its main bulletin with the launch of Xi's new book, a selection of his "most important and fundamental works".

Foreign journalists cannot travel to Tibet without government permission. We have just a few hours to get as much information as we can on huge stories like this before videos are scrubbed and voices stifled.

Instead, we have to rely on state media, which has so far focused on incredibly dramatic rescue efforts.

Specialist search teams scaling mountains and cliff faces, or crossing raging rivers to try to get to the worst-affected areas. We don't yet know what happened afterwards, or who they were able to save.

This is not to say that Beijing is unconcerned. Rather, they are very concerned.

China's Premier Li Qiang was quickly despatched to the region, where he was seen inspecting debris removal - a rare visit by the country's second-most important leader so soon after a major disaster.

The reason for what the world might see as a muted response is to preserve the one thing Xi covets for his country: stability.

The Communist Party will fear that such a disaster could fuel discontent, either with the response or the lack of foresight to prevent it.

It may also fear the impact of a tragedy like this and its potential to be a rallying factor, especially in a community where faith has long played a central role.

Although the region has not seen protests in a long time, Tibetan groups abroad have expressed concern over increasing Chinese control, such as new education laws that they say aim to weaken the role of monasteries and the Buddhist faith.

Just hours after the disaster struck, the Communist Party machine tried to rally its grassroots to stem any signs of discontent of its handling of the landslide.

A notice came from the local party office urging members to step up and help in disaster relief efforts in their area and provide emotional guidance or psychological support to affected residents.

The key line instructs them to "make every effort to maintain social order and ensure stability and public confidence in the disaster areas". Those who perform well would be rewarded - and those who do badly "would be held accountable".

It is a warning that will not be taken lightly. Tibetans in the region can be detained or arrested for speaking to journalists or posting anything online that is seen as contrary to the government narrative, according to rights activists.

That is making it difficult for Tibetans outside the region to find out what has happened to their relatives.

The International Campaign for Tibet, while praising the work of first responders in the area, said Beijing had been removing videos and other first-hand information from social media. It called on Chinese authorities to "disclose complete and verifiable information about the damage and casualties".

To try to understand what life is like for Tibetans, the BBC travelled to a town that sits on the edge of the Himalayan plateau last year - just outside what China calls the Tibetan Autonomous region.

There, we spoke to monks at the Kirti monastery in Aba, or Ngaba in Tibetan, which was once at the heart of its resistance to Beijing. "We Tibetans are denied basic human rights," one monk told us.

They said they lived under constant surveillance and claimed the Chinese government oppressed and persecuted Tibetans. The conversations were brief because we could not be seen speaking to anyone for long.

Beijing denies it is violating Tibetans' rights, and points to the heavy investments it has made in the region to boost tourism and integrate it with the rest of the country.

Nevertheless, people in China will not know very much about what is happening in Tibet right now.

articles.title: Sleeper teams from each Power 4 conference: Who will exceed expectations this college football season?
articles.summary: Virginia Tech, Houston, Washington and Mississippi State lead the 2026 college football sleeper teams poised to upset the Power 4 conference order.
articles.body: With college football beginning in earnest this Saturday, many fans are anxiously awaiting to see how the chips will fall in a wide open season in 2026. Sure, on paper, there is a clear delineation between the teams who have everything to win a national championship and the rest of the field, but as they always say, "paper never played a football game." With that in mind, I wanted to take a look at some of my favorite sleeper teams from each Power 4 conference. PREDICTING EACH POWER 4 CONFERENCE CHAMPION AHEAD OF THE 2026 COLLEGE FOOTBALL SEASON I already discussed who I think is going to win each conference, but what about the teams no one sees coming that could upset the established order. These aren't necessarily teams that I would put money on to win their respective conferences, but they are certainly could if things break the right way. Let's take a look at some power conference teams who are flying under the radar this season. ACC - Virginia Tech Hokies I wrote an entire article about how shocked I was to see the Hokies not in the preseason top-25, and I was even more shocked to see they were projected to finish 8th in the ACC. I understand it hasn't exactly been a bed of roses for Virginia Tech since legendary coach Frank Beamer retired, but the Hokies — at least to my eye — have everything they need to finish in the upper echelon of the ACC this season. For starters, landing head coach James Franklin was an absolute coup. RANKING THE TEN BEST COLLEGE FOOTBALL COACHES IN THE COUNTRY AHEAD OF THE 2026 SEASON I know I haven't been the most vocal defender of Franklin, but I still think he's a hell of a coach who will benefit from a change of scenery and a slightly less competitive conference. The Hokies also rank top-five in the country in returning production and will feature Franklin's handpicked signal caller Ethan Grunkemeyer under center. Grunkemeyer was forced into action after Penn State starter Drew Allar was lost for the season midway through 2025, and that experience will be invaluable for Virginia Tech this season. A soft start to their schedule could provide the perfect "ramp up" into the meat of their slate in late October, and I wouldn't be shocked at all to see the Hokies push teams like SMU and Louisville for that silver medal spot in the ACC this year. Big 12 - Houston Cougars Everyone knows about Texas Tech and the stockpile of talent they have out in Lubbock, but I'm keeping my eye on another team on the opposite end of the Lone Star State to make some noise in the Big 12. I'm surprised I haven't heard more about the Cougars during the preseason hype sessions, considering they won 10 games and finished in the top-25 last season, but perhaps this is right where they want to be. Houston has all the ingredients to challenge the Red Raiders for the conference crown, including a great coach in Willie Fritz, an ascending defense, and one of the most experienced rosters in the Big 12 heading into 2026. A massive early-season showdown looms between the Cougars and the Red Raiders in September, and if Houston is able to keep that game close or even win it, it could be the statement they need to let everyone know they are for real. Other than the aforementioned date with Texas Tech, Houston avoids many of the other heavy hitters in the Big 12, including BYU and both Arizona schools, so another 10-win season could be in the books in H-Town. Big Ten - Washington Huskies I think the world of Washington head coach Jedd Fisch, and even wanted him to replace Billy Napier at Florida before Jon Sumrall was hired, so it's no surprise I believe he and the Huskies could achieve big things this year. Looking at Fisch's trajectory, both at Arizona and now at Washington, will give fans a glimpse into what they could expect from the Huskies in 2026. THREE TEAMS RANKED OUTSIDE THE TOP-12 OF THE COACHES POLL WHO WILL MAKE THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF The Wildcats went from one win to five wins to 10 wins in three seasons under Fisch, and the current Washington head coach had win totals of six and nine in his first two seasons in Seattle, respectively. With dynamic quarterback Demond Williams Jr. returning as well as a roster that ranks in the top-15 nationally in returning production, Fisch has all the pieces in place to make a legitimate run at a Big Ten title or, at the very least, put together a remarkable season in the Pacific Northwest. Washington avoids Michigan and Ohio State this year and will play Penn State and Indiana at home. A forgivable schedule could help the Huskies outperform their preseason expectations and have a lot of critics eating crow by season's end. SEC - Mississippi State Bulldogs As far as SEC sleepers go, I've seen plenty of love for programs like South Carolina, Auburn, and even Kentucky, but for my money, I believe the Mississippi State Bulldogs will shock plenty of fans and media pundits alike in 2026. Jeff Lebby enters his third season as the head coach in Starkville, and many will view his 2025 season as a failure upon first glance. The losing record will cause many to believe the rebuild is behind schedule, but a closer look shows that the Bulldogs were a few bad bounces and missteps away from an eight-win season. Mississippi State took both Texas and Tennessee — two top-25 teams — to overtime, and were a terrible interception in field goal range away from beating Florida in The Swamp. The Bulldogs are a sneaky talented team, shockingly ranking in the top-20 of the 247Sports Team Talent Composite, as Lebby has done a remarkable job upgrading the personnel at Mississippi State. Sophomore quarterback Kamario Taylor was a highly-touted player coming out of high school and will unlock Lebby's offense with his combination of plus athleticism and uncanny arm talent. articles.title: Far-right UK provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos detained by ICE in US
articles.summary: A Trump administration official says the controversial commentator overstayed his visit in the US and will be removed.
articles.body:
Milo Yiannopoulos, a far-right British commentator known for previously being a vocal supporter of United States President Donald Trump, has been detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

A spokesperson for the US Department of Homeland Security told Al Jazeera that Yiannopoulos was taken into custody at the Louis Armstrong International Airport in New Orleans, Louisiana, on Thursday.

He allegedly overstayed his legal authorisation to remain in the US after entering the country through New York City on May 14, 2019.

“Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an Immigration Judge on July 22, after failing to show up for his immigration hearing,” the spokesperson wrote on Friday. “He will remain in ICE custody pending removal.”

The Department of Homeland Security also posted a photo to social media that appeared to be a mugshot of the 41-year-old conservative firebrand who, in June 2025, called on the Trump administration to “deport millions and millions and millions of people”.

In the post, the department warned that those detained for overstaying their visit would be “arrested and deported without a chance to return”.

Online records do not specify which ICE detention facility is currently holding Yiannopoulos. Instead, it refers “family members and legal representatives” to contact the ICE field office in Alexandria, Louisiana, for additional details.

Reports indicate Yiannopoulos was in New Orleans for a concert by the musician Ye, formerly known as Kanye West. TMZ was the first to report Yiannopoulos’s detainment.

Laura Loomer, a top Trump ally known for spreading conspiracy theories, appeared to take credit for Yiannopoulos’s detainment, calling it a “great day for America”.

She also denounced Yiannopoulos’s work with former US Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene, a Trump supporter-turned-critic.

“I was the first person to report on the fact that Milo was in the US illegally where he incited violence against President Trump and worked for Marjorie Traitor Greene,” Loomer wrote on the social media platform X. “When Milo called for me to be assassinated, I reported him to ICE and FBI.”

Loomer has publicly sparred with Yiannopoulos for years. He previously exposed what he purported to be Loomer’s mental health struggles in a September 2024 post, claiming she had been involuntarily committed to psychiatric facilities.

Yiannopoulos, known for his online trolling and anti-Islamic postings, was permanently banned by X’s predecessor, Twitter, in July 2016. His account was reinstated when Elon Musk took over the company.

After that, Yiannopoulos returned to the platform with a series of inflammatory posts, including one that called the “Muslim world functionally retarded”.

More recently, the 41-year-old founded a Los Angeles-based talent management called Tarantula that offers, in its own words, “unrivalled connections, capital and expertise” to a host of celebrities and public figures.

The site lists a number of controversial “past and present” clients like Trump, Ye, convicted fraudster “Pharma Bro” Martin Shkreli and rapper Azealia Banks.

articles.title: U.S. enters deal with Venezuela to take control of 65 billion barrels of oil reserves, Trump says
articles.summary: President Donald Trump announced Friday that the U.S. had entered into an agreement with Venezuela to take control of the country’s 65 billion barrels of oil reserves.
articles.body: President Donald Trump announced Friday that the U.S. had entered into an agreement with Venezuela to take control of the country’s 65 billion barrels of oil reserves. “BREAKING NEWS: The United States of America has just entered into an Agreement with the Country of Venezuela on, THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY! At my direction, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, working closely with Highly Respected Interim President of Venezuela, Delcy Rodriguez, and, through a partnership with private business, have secured majority U.S. control of more than 65 BILLION BARRELS of proven Oil Reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the American Taxpayer,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. Trump added that the transaction “MORE THAN DOUBLES American Oil Reserves.” In January, the U.S. military carried out an operation to capture Venezuela’s President Nicolás Maduro to face federal narcoterrorism and drug trafficking charges in the U.S. Trump is facing increasing pressure as the midterms loom and gas prices have spiked because of the war with Iran, which the U.S. and Israel started exactly six months ago. Secretary of State Marco Rubio touted the deal as a “huge win” for both the U.S. and Venezuela in a post on X. “It demonstrates how President Trump’s bold foreign policy is driving America First wins: securing stable reserves and low-cost oil in our Hemisphere and lowering gas prices here at home,” he wrote. “For the Venezuelan people, this deal will bring nearly $100 billion in private investment, support thousands of high-paying jobs, and drive the reconstruction of Venezuela’s economy.” Venezuela has among the largest oil reserves in the world, with an estimated 303 billion barrels of crude oil in the ground. That’s about 17% of the world’s supply, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Unlike other parts of the world, where geologists have to search for untapped oil, the reserves under Venezuela’s soil are largely mapped and known, experts say. But because of dilapidated infrastructure, the country only produces about 1% of the world’s oil.

articles.title: CBC releases policy change after controversy about refusing to refer to 9/11 as  ‘terrorist attacks’
articles.summary: The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's leaked memo told journalists not to call 9/11 a terrorist attack, sparking outrage before the anniversary.
articles.body: The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation announced an internal policy change Friday, explaining why it had previously told reporters and editors to refrain from describing the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks as "terrorist attacks." The memo was authored by Basem Boshra, CBC News' senior director of journalistic standards and public trust, and surfaced ahead of the attacks' 25th anniversary. The directive was first reported by Toronto Sun columnist Warren Kinsella, who said it was addressed to CBC News staff. "Do not refer to the Sept. 11 attacks as terrorist attacks," the memo said. The memo instead described the events as hijackings that led to passenger jet crashes in Washington, D.C., Pennsylvania and Manhattan. It also said the World Trade Center was destroyed. AMERICA’S HEARTLAND COMES FACE-TO-FACE WITH 9/11 HISTORY AS 25TH ANNIVERSARY NEARS CBC released a memo Friday addressing the controversy that erupted as the 25th anniversary of the terror attack, headlined, "How and why CBC News will adjust its 9/11 language guidance." "CBC News finds itself once again in a swirl of confusion about how our journalists use the words ‘terrorist’ and ‘terrorism,’ this time about the al-Qaeda attacks on New York, Washington, D.C., and Pennsylvania on Sept. 11, 2001," it said. "The confusion stems from the leak of an excerpt from our internal language guide that was published and amplified by a number of outlets without full context or explanation. It has caused significant concern, anger and hurt for many people who believe CBC News seeks to minimize or obscure the horror of that day and who was behind it," Boshra continued. "That is the last thing we want to do. And our reporting on 9/11, through thousands of stories over the past 25 years, is an unflinching account of the devastating attacks by al-Qaeda, the hunt and prosecution of those responsible, the thousands of lives that were lost on that day and the incalculable loss and grief experienced by so many others as a result. "And we intend to mark the forthcoming 25th anniversary of 9/11 with extensive, special coverage that will continue to respectfully and thoughtfully reflect on the monumental nature of this tragedy. SYRIA OFF US TERROR BLACKLIST AFTER NEARLY 50 YEARS AS TRUMP ADMIN CLEARS INVESTMENT HURDLE "CBC's reporting on terrorism, wherever it occurs, has always been guided by the principle of attribution, and like other major news organizations, it has been our practice for decades," he explained. "The reason for the extreme care around the use of the words ‘terrorist’ and ‘terrorism’ was detailed in this earlier editor's blog. "But to be clear, CBC News has never said what happened on Sept. 11, 2001, was not terrorism, as some commentators have stated in recent days. We have reported fully and accurately on the reasons and motivations for those attacks as determined by police, governments and an independent commission. We've just made sure to do it with attribution," he said. "Clarity and understanding are at the heart of our journalism. The leaked excerpt without context or explanation has raised more questions for the public that we must now answer," he said. "After reviewing our current language guidance, we have decided to adjust it to clarify that direct attribution is not required for describing the historic events of 9/11 as terrorism. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We are doing so to remove what has unfortunately (and unintentionally) become an impediment to clarity and public understanding," he concluded. "At the same time, as new acts of politically or ideologically motivated violence occur in our world, we will continue to follow the journalistically sound practice of attributing causes and motivations to officials and experts." Lt. Col. Michael Schrama, a military judge, on Friday threw out a confession made by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the alleged mastermind of the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks. In his ruling, Schrama wrote that statements made by Mohammed to investigators in 2007 were not given voluntarily, according to the New York Post, complicating what has already been a decades-long wait for the suspected plotter to stand trial. Earlier this week, Schrama set a trial date for June 2028 for Mohammed and three co-defendants. Fox News' C.J. Womack and Louis Casiano contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump hails 'historic' deal for US to control 65bn barrels of Venezuela's oil
articles.summary: Venezuelan interim president says the unusual agreement will help revive her country's economy.
articles.body:
The US has reached a deal with Venezuela to control more than 65 billion barrels of its proven oil reserves, President Donald Trump announced.

"This Historic Transaction MORE THAN DOUBLES American Oil Reserves, greatly increases our Oil Supply, and will substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans," Trump posted on social media.

Venezuela's interim President, Delcy Rodriguez, hailed the agreement as one that would help her nation's economic revival.

Trump vowed to tap Venezuela's reserves, the world's largest, after the US captured its then-President Nicolás Maduro this year. More recently, Trump has been under pressure to tame domestic petrol prices, which spiked amid the Iran conflict.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the oil deal "a huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people". Details have not been released.

"For the Venezuelan people, this deal will bring nearly $100 billion in private investment, support thousands of high-paying jobs, and drive the reconstruction of Venezuela's economy," Rubio said on social media.

In his post, Trump said Rubio and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth had reached the agreement with Venezuela's leadership "through a partnership with private business".

He did not elaborate on the partnership or describe possible commitments and terms for the US in the deal, but he claimed the agreement was reached "at no cost to the American Taxpayer".

Venezuela's interim President Rodriguez said in a statement that the agreement would have "a significant impact on our nation' revival", by bringing in investment in the infrastructure needed to develop its hydrocarbon industry.

The deal calls for the development of 17 strategic oil fields with a proven potential of 65 billion barrels, as well as "an investment of more than $100 billion, and more than $209 billion in taxes for the State", Rodriguez said.

"These investments will contribute not only to the recovery and modernization of our industry, but also to our country's economic growth, the energy security of our hemisphere, and greater balance in international markets," she said.

Under the deal the US government will retain 55% control of a joint venture with an "experienced private operator in Venezuela", a US official told the BBC's media partner CBS News.

Rodriguez gave the venture a 100-year concession to operate in the oil fields, according to the official.

Trump gave few details of the highly unusual agreement, which appears to grant the US direct governance over a foreign country's sovereign national resources.

The deal would appear to be wider in scope than the US-led Coalition Provisional Authority's control over Iraq's oil revenues after Saddam Hussein was ousted in an American-led invasion in 2003.

But it is unclear whether the Venezuela agreement could face legal and constitutional challenges in the South American nation.

Then-President Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, were seized in a US special forces operation authorised by Trump on 3 January.

In the hours after the raid, Trump said his administration would run Venezuela until a "safe, proper and judicious transition" could take place, adding that the US would indefinitely control the sale of the country's oil.

Venezuela has the largest proven oil reserves in the world - an estimated 303 billion barrels. However, production has plummeted since its peak in the late 1990s.

Trump has asked US oil firms to invest at least $100bn (£75bn) to restore the country's oil industry.

He has also claimed the rights to Venezuela's oil after alleging that the country had in the past "unilaterally seized and sold American oil, American assets and American platforms, costing us billions and billions of dollars".
