articles.summary: In the months before Lindsay Clancy killed her three children and tried to take her own life, she was desperate for help — she saw psychiatrists, called a suicide hotline, went to the emergency room and was turned away from inpatient treatment.
articles.body: In the months before Lindsay Clancy killed her three children and tried to take her own life, she was desperate for help — she saw psychiatrists, called a suicide hotline, went to the emergency room and was turned away from inpatient treatment. She was put on 13 medications over four months as providers sought to treat her ongoing symptoms and adverse reactions to the medications. Clancy, 36, is accused of murdering her three children — Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callan, 8 months — on Jan. 24, 2023, before she threw herself out her bedroom window in a suicide attempt. Prosecutors spent nearly six weeks presenting their case to jurors in the murder trial. They called 70 witnesses in an attempt to show that the mother planned the deaths, driving her husband from home so she could carry out the acts. Her defense attorneys have said that Clancy was in the grips of postpartum psychosis, a rare condition that can alter new mothers’ sense of reality and is considered a psychiatric emergency. Her condition, they told jurors, compelled her to act on the voices in her head that were telling her to kill her three children and herself. For months, she had been seeking help from doctors and medical professionals. The prosecution and defense made their closing arguments Thursday, and the jury began deliberating that afternoon. The trial has raised questions about the type of care Clancy received. Clancy’s medical providers have said they adjusted her treatment as needed and based on her responses to the medications she was prescribed. At times, the medical providers testified, they did not have full access to her medical record and did not coordinate with one another. It was also unclear when Clancy stopped taking medications and began to take new ones. Dr. Veerle Bergink, the director of Mount Sinai’s Women’s Mental Health Center, told NBC News that testimony about Clancy’s providers shows that “during multiple occasions, the diagnosis was missed and she did not get the right treatment.” Bergink, who specializes in mental health during pregnancy and postpartum, said Clancy’s adverse reaction to the antidepressants she was taking could have been “a major clue” that her diagnosis went beyond postpartum depression and that she needed different medication for postpartum psychosis. Dr. Tracy Moran Vozar, a psychologist and perinatal mental health expert, said Clancy’s case exemplifies the systemic issues and lack of communication across the healthcare system, especially when it comes to patients with serious mental illness who see multiple providers across different systems. Neither doctor personally treated Clancy. “It’s very tragic, of course, for her, her family, and everything that happened,” Bergink said. “But it’s a tragedy for doctors, as well.” Court testimony and documents from the trial provide a timeline of the care Clancy sought and received in the months before the killings. September 2022 On Sept. 15, 2022, Clancy first met with Dr. Jennifer Tufts, a psychiatrist at Aster Mental Health, more than three months after her youngest child, Callan, was born. Tufts treated Clancy through January 2023. Clancy reported she was experiencing anxiety attacks, depressed mood, being unable to feel pleasure, guilt, decreased appetite, racing thoughts and other symptoms, Tufts testified in court. She said Clancy responded “no” to questions about whether she was hearing voices or having thoughts about harming herself or others. Tufts diagnosed Clancy with generalized anxiety disorder and an adjustment disorder with depressed mood, which is when someone is reacting or struggling with a stressful change more intensely than expected. She also prescribed Clancy a standard dose of the antidepressant sertraline, known by the brand name Zoloft, at a dose of 25 milligrams, then increased to 50 mg. Tufts testified that Clancy had previously taken Zoloft for about a week after the birth of her second child, according to NBC Boston. October Tufts testified that in October, Clancy felt “awful” after her dose of Zoloft was increased and that she was feeling more depressed, “crying all day” and having trouble eating and sleeping, among other symptoms, according to NBC Boston. “Anxiety was really bad even before med, now hard to differentiate. Overnight racing thoughts, paranoid of getting suicidal thoughts, something bad happening. Doesn’t want to be alone,” Tufts said, reading from her records, according to NBC Boston. Tufts said she was “very concerned” about Clancy at this point. She told Clancy to stop taking the Zoloft. Through the end of the month, Tufts and Clancy met again, and she was prescribed the benzodiazepine lorazepam, known by the brand name Ativan, the anti-anxiety medication buspirone and the antihistamine hydroxyzine, according to the defense and court testimony. November Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington said at the trial that Clancy had gotten much worse by the next appointment on Nov. 2, despite the medications she was taking, according to NBC Boston. Reddington said Tufts said that Clancy’s insomnia had increased, that she had anxiety and that she was worrying about suicide. Tufts testified that during that appointment, she said Clancy was “improving” and therefore decreased the Ativan, according to NBC Boston. Tufts responded to Reddington that she did not recall that the symptoms were significantly aggravated. On Nov. 16, Clancy went to the South Shore Hospital emergency room, where she was prescribed the antidepressant trazodone. Days later, on Nov. 21, psychiatric nurse practitioner Julie Paul saw Clancy at South Shore Perinatal Behavioral Health clinic after Clancy’s former mother-in-law contacted the doctor, according to NBC Boston. Paul prescribed the antidepressant fluoxetine, known under the brand name Prozac, at 10 mg. Paul testified that during this time, Clancy “was feeling overwhelmed” and that she had increased anxiety as her husband returned to work after the birth of their child. Clancy also described having issues with sleeping. During a follow-up visit the next day, Tufts testified, Clancy denied having any suicidal ideation. On Nov. 25, Paul prescribed Clancy the antidepressant mirtazapine, known by the brand name Remeron, at 5 mg; the benzodiazepine clonazepam, known as the brand name Klonopin, at 0.5 mg; and the anti-insomnia medication zolpidem, known by the brand name Ambien, according to the defense. At this time, Clancy also reported having had an adverse reaction to Prozac, according to the defense. Clancy told Paul she was feeling disconnected and “spacey” after having taken the medication, according to Paul’s testimony, so they switched to mirtazapine. Clancy reported dissociation and confusion to her care team on Nov. 28 after having taken Remeron, according to a defense timeline of when Clancy sought care. Two days later, psychiatric nurse practitioner Rebecca Jollotta prescribed the antipsychotic Seroquel at 25 mg. Jollotta took over Clancy’s care after Paul left South Shore Perinatal Behavioral Health clinic. December In December, Clancy also continued meeting with Tufts. As her symptoms continued, she called a suicide crisis hotline and sought inpatient treatment — which she was turned away from, according to the defense and trial testimony. Tufts said that during a visit on Dec. 1, Clancy denied feeling suicidal but felt “close to being suicidal.” Clancy said she was having difficulty sleeping because of the multiple medications she was taking, Tufts said. Clancy told Tufts she had “worse depression and intrusive thoughts” after having taken Remeron, along with “the feeling that I was going to die,” according to court testimony. Reddington, Clancy’s lawyer, asked Tufts at the trial, “You’ve got a woman telling you she’s hopeless, she doesn’t care if she dies, she can’t sleep. What did you do to validate your therapy?” “I told her that this was something we could address, there was hope, there were treatments,” Tufts replied, according to NBC Boston. They also discussed the possibility of undiagnosed bipolar disorder, with Tufts testifying that Clancy did not appear to have mania at the time. On Dec. 2, Clancy returned to the South Shore Hospital behavioral clinic. Latiesha Dukes, a perinatal clinician who provided short-term therapy for Clancy, said that during her intake appointment, Clancy presented with concerns of anxiety, lack of sleep and thoughts of wanting to die, according to NBC Boston. Dukes testified that Clancy reported “having low mood and feeling numb” during the appointment. She said she met with Clancy four times and did not observe any signs of mania or psychosis. She said she referred Clancy to Women & Infants Hospital in Rhode Island because of “continued passive suicidal ideation.” Clancy went to the hospital but was discharged. On Dec. 4, Clancy called a suicide crisis hotline. She met with Dukes again the next day and told her that she had called the Aspire crisis line and was evaluated by a clinician but was told “she did not meet the criteria for inpatient treatment due to not having any suicidal ideation plan,” Dukes testified. From Dec. 6 to Dec. 13, Jollotta prescribed the benzodiazepine diazepam, known by the brand name Valium, at different doses and also increased Clancy’s Seroquel dose. Days later, on Dec. 15, Patrick Clancy contacted providers to report worsening symptoms, according to the defense’s timeline chart. The next day, Clancy met with Tufts, when, according to Tufts’ testimony, Clancy was “sleeping but she was still feeling very poorly.” Tufts testified that Clancy continued to feel hopeless and depressed and had some suicidal ideation but that she denied having a plan to hurt herself. Tufts prescribed the mood stabilizer lamotrigine, known by the brand name Lamictal. “While she was certainly struggling, she did not require hospitalization at that point,” Tufts said, according to NBC Boston. Reddington asked Tufts on the stand whether she knew Clancy had told her then-husband that she was having thoughts about harming the children, according to NBC Boston. “I would have been very concerned if I had heard that,” Tufts said. On Dec. 19, Jollotta increased Clancy’s Seroquel dose. The next day, Clancy visited the Massachusetts General Hospital emergency room, according to a chart from the defense. Over the next few days, she was evaluated for and participated in the Women and Infants Partial Hospitalization Program for patients with postpartum depression, according to the defense’s chart. Jollotta lowered Clancy’s Seroquel dose. But by Dec. 30, Clancy had returned to the Massachusetts General Hospital emergency room, according to the defense’s chart. January 2023 On New Year’s Day, Clancy arrived at McLean Hospital from the emergency department at Massachusetts General Hospital. Dr. Alia Goodheart, a psychiatrist, testified that Clancy’s main complaint was that she was having trouble sleeping and felt “numb,” according to NBC Boston. Clancy also complained that she was having side effects from the medication she was taking. Two days later, Clancy met Goodheart for the first time. Goodheart testified that Clancy said she was feeling “numbness” but did not indicate any plan for suicide, according to NBC Boston. Goodheart said in court that the potential for a bipolar disorder diagnosis came up during the sessions. She said she did not observe signs of psychosis from Clancy. On Jan. 5, Clancy left McLean Hospital. She had been prescribed trazodone and Ativan. Goodheart testified that she did not have concerns about her safety or worry that she was a risk to anyone else. Clancy had an appointment with Tufts the day after she left McLean Hospital. She was diagnosed with “major depression,” Tufts said at the trial, according to NBC Boston. She continued to report numbness and having trouble sleeping, Tufts testified. From Jan. 9 through Jan. 16, Tufts adjusted Clancy’s prescriptions, including prescribing her Valium at different doses and trazadone, and Jollotta also prescribed her Valium, according to the defense’s chart. On Jan. 16, Clancy had another appointment with Tufts, who prescribed the antidepressant amitriptyline. Clancy again told Tufts she was feeling numb and that bonding with her infant son felt forced, Tufts testified, according to NBC Boston. Tufts said she was “concerned that she was depressed.” Clancy had her last appointment with Tufts on Jan. 23. Tufts testified that Clancy still had a depressed mood and felt numb and that she said she had to force herself out of bed, according to NBC Boston. Tufts testified that Clancy reported no signs of suicidal or homicidal ideation and showed no signs of psychosis. The next day, authorities allege, she killed her three children and tried to die by suicide. articles.title: Woman allegedly ejected from roller coaster, suffers serious injuries after dragged along track: reports
articles.summary: Nicki Parker, 60, was dragged 20 to 30 seconds along the Rocky Mountain Coaster track at Copper Mountain Resort after being ejected from her seat, an attorney claims.
articles.body: A 60-year-old woman suffered a broken rib, collapsed lung, a traumatic brain injury and a dislocated shoulder that required surgery after she was allegedly ejected from her seat on a Colorado roller coaster and dragged, according to reports and a law firm representing her. Nicki Parker of Texas was thrown from her seat and dragged for 20 to 30 seconds after she remained strapped into her seat belt as the Rocky Mountain Coaster at Copper Mountain Resort kept going, FOX 31 Denver reported, citing her attorney. "It was actually wrapped around her and pulled her, and she was dragged along the track as it went down," Trent Ongert of the Bloch Ongert Injury Law told the news station. MONTANA BOY KILLED AFTER BEING FLUNG FROM CARNIVAL RIDE OPERATING WITH MISSING RESTRAINTS, LAWSUIT ALLEGES Ongert said Parker’s husband, who was riding behind her at the time, attempted to help her. "She was lying on the track. He then had to get her out because there was nobody, no way to get to her," he explained. "They’re about 15 to 20 feet off the ground." Parker remains hospitalized, Ongert said. A sign posted along the ride says that the "cart will stop and beep" if a seat belt is disconnected. COLLEGE GRAD REPORTEDLY DIES IN SIX FLAGS ROLLER COASTER INCIDENT AS FAMILY SUES THEME PARK Colorado’s Division of Oil and Public Safety's Amusement Rides and Devices Program is investigating the incident. "We can confirm our Division of Oil & Public Safety is investigating an incident that happened on Copper Mountain's Rocky Mountain Coaster on Monday, August 17, 2026," the agency told Fox News Digital. "One rider was injured in the incident. The Rocky Mountain Coaster is currently closed while the investigation continues. OPS has also told the manufacturer that they need to publish a safety bulletin and share it with all impacted operators. "A similar ride operating at the Purgatory Resort is also closed pending the outcome of the investigation. Documentation involving the incident will not be made public until the investigation is complete." JURY AWARDS TEENS $550K AFTER OREGON AMUSEMENT PARK RIDE LEFT THEM HANGING UPSIDE DOWN: REPORT The roller coaster, which is 5,800 feet long and bills itself as the "2nd longest alpine coaster in North America," remains closed, according to its website. articles.title: Baltics downplay threat after CIA chief’s ‘warning to Russia’ on Nato
articles.summary: Europe News: Leaders of Estonia and Latvia sought to play down the significance of a rare visit to Moscow by CIA chief John Ratcliffe, saying the threat Russia pos.
articles.body: Leaders of Estonia and Latvia sought to play down the significance of a rare visit to Moscow by CIA chief John Ratcliffe, saying the threat Russia poses to the region hasn’t changed.“Throughout Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, US officials have met regularly with Russian representatives, so the CIA director’s visit should not be regarded as pivotal,” Estonian foreign minister Margus Tsahkna said in a statement Thursday. Separately, Latvian PM Andris Kulbergs said there “is currently no reason for concern.”The trip followed warnings from intelligence officials that Russian security services are looking at hybrid warfare operations, which could include infrastructure sabotage or false-flag attacks, against the Baltic states and Poland.The Wall Street Journal and Politico reported Wednesday that the purpose of Ratcliffe’s meetings was to warn Moscow not to attack Nato countries, particularly the Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lit­huania. The CIA hasn’t co­mm­ented. President Trump said on Wednesday that Ratcliffe was in Moscow on a “semi-routine basis,” but did­n’t elaborate on the purpose of the visit. The head of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, Sergei Naryshkin, said the meeting took place in a “working format” and the two spy chiefs discussed issues within the remit of intelligence agencies, ac­cording to Interfax.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Somali piracy surges as the impact of the US-Iran war ripples outwards
articles.summary: Two ships were seized within four days last week raising to at least 13 the number attacked since January.
articles.body:
A surge in piracy near Somalia has increased threats to shipping already under pressure from maritime blockades and conflict due to the US war with Iran.

Two cargo vessels were seized in the Gulf of Aden within four days last week, rising to at least 13 the number of ships attacked since the start of the year and triggering unprecedented drone strikes against the pirates.

It is the biggest escalation in hijackings in more than a decade, renewing concern about security in this region vital to international trade.

"Piracy is always a crime of opportunity," says Omar Mahmood, a senior Somalia analyst for the International Crisis Group (ICG), "and right now the pirates see an opportunity."

That opportunity comes from the impact of the war on regional waterways further north.

Iran and the US continue to battle over control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz.

And Tehran's Houthi allies in Yemen have imposed a targeted blockade in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which controls access to the Red Sea. This is focused on a dispute with Saudi Arabia but heightens insecurity for international shipping.

"I guess the pirates believe that with those two external events in Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, they believe that the international forces will be dedicated to those crises instead of looking for pirates," says Vice-Admiral Ignacio Villanueva Serrano, operation commander for the European Union's naval force that protects shipping off Somalia's coast.

Among the latest vessels hijacked by the pirates was a Cameroon-flagged ship, the MV Lutuf, which was attacked off the coast of Somalia's semi-autonomous Puntland region on 17 August. A few days later pirates boarded an oil products tanker, the Eritrean-flagged MT Sibu 1, in waters near Yemen, on the other side of the Gulf.

The capture of the Lutuf has triggered unexpected consequences.

Thirteen men allegedly belonging to a network that supplies the pirates on the ship have been killed in two drone strikes since 18 August. No one has said they are behind the attacks, but local officials blamed them on Turkey, saying the vessel was carrying Turkish weapons.

The Lutuf is now among six vessels being held for demands of millions of dollars in ransom, four of which are anchored near the fishing town of Bander Beyla known as a hotbed for piracy, the BBC has learned.

That is nowhere near the peak levels of hijackings 15 years ago that cost the global economy billions of dollars. In 2011 Somali pirates carried out more than 200 attacks and held hundreds of crew members hostage.

A co-ordinated international naval response together with private security on commercial ships successfully drove down the scourge and contained a flare-up in 2023 and 2024.

But experts stress that while the pirate networks were suppressed, they remained intact, given the failure to address the poor economic and security conditions in Somalia that feed them.

Currently the resurgence is fuelled locally by anger over foreign trawlers which overfish in Somali waters, damaging the fishing industry that sustains communities in Puntland.

And there are more targets available now with a potentially bigger payload.

The regional maritime insecurity has driven some ships closer to the Somali coast as they divert south to avoid the conflict further north. Given the high price of oil, hijacking a tanker is more lucrative.

"You have that combined effect of less naval patrolling but more commercial shipping in these waters," according to the analyst Mahmood, "and that signals an opportunity.

"And once you've had a successful attack, I think that spurs other units to do copycat type incidents as well."

He and other researchers suspect there may be collaboration between the Somali pirates and Yemenis after several vessels were seized near Yemen's coast.

But Mahmood says these would more likely be criminal elements than Iran's Houthi allies, especially as one of the ships seized last week, the MT Sibu 1, allegedly belonged to an Iranian "shadow fleet" used to transport petroleum products trying to dodge US sanctions.

"I don't see something specifically Iran-directed," he says.

Turkey, however, reportedly has a stake in the latest hijackings.

Puntland security sources and a Somali government official have told the BBC that the Lutuf was carrying weapons bound for a Turkish military training facility in the Somali capital, Mogadishu. Ankara has an agreement with Somalia to strengthen its maritime security, as part of a wider defence and economic partnership.

The security sources say six international warships are now in the seas close to the Lutuf - two from Turkey and one each from Spain, Denmark, the US and India, something the BBC has not been able to independently verify.

"There is military equipment on the [hijacked] ship meant for Turkey's operations in Somalia," the Somali government official said, speaking on condition of anonymity, adding that the cargo included satellite equipment for a space station that Ankara is building north of the capital.

He alleged that Turkey had carried out the second drone strike that killed nine armed men on Sunday.

"The men who were killed were criminals and I don't have sympathy for them," he said, "but taking it to that level is escalating the situation even more."

Turkey's defence ministry has stated that its forces are providing "necessary support" to Somali authorities regarding the incident involving a hijacked vessel in Somali territorial waters, within the framework of their security agreement. But it stopped short of addressing the accusations that Turkey had carried out deadly drone strikes.

Publicly the government in Mogadishu has said only that it is aware of the operations against pirate groups and will take measures to address them.

Puntland authorities have been more outspoken.

Speaking to the BBC's Somali Service, Deputy Minister of Security Abdirahman Yusuf said his administration had evidence that Turkey was responsible for the attacks, citing information about Turkish activity around the vessel and along the Puntland coast.

The BBC has not independently verified his allegations.

The security ministry also issued a statement expressing opposition to "bombings by international warships targeting civilians" that "undermined co-operation… in combatting piracy", and demanded an immediate explanation for why they were carried out.

Puntland is wary of Turkey's close military relationship with the Somali government, and the incidents risk further complicating a long-standing political dispute between the semi-autonomous region and Mogadishu that hinders a co-ordinated effort to fight piracy, analysts say.

There is not yet a full-blown resurgence. But without an end to the US-Iran war, or increased international efforts at deterrence, Somali piracy stands to continue raising the threat level in a crucial maritime space that is already dangerously squeezed.

articles.title: Box breathing: Inside the 'most powerful hack' to control stress
articles.summary: We spoke to experts about how the breathing technique used by soldiers and influencers works.
articles.body:
Powerless to help after catastrophic earthquakes struck her hometown of La Guaira in Venezuela two months ago, Maria Medina struggled to sleep.

She was more than 1,500 miles away in Florida, USA - where she has lived for the last 15 years - and was racked with worry for family and friends.

Box breathing helped her combat sleepless nights.

"In moments where I feel that there isn't much that I can do, like lying in bed at night and staring at the ceiling... I know it's going to help me," she says.

The 31-year-old first came across box breathing in 2020. She was studying for a master's degree while working full-time and the stress of doing both became too much once the Covid pandemic hit .

She sought help from a therapist who showed her how to box breathe.

The technique consists of inhaling for four seconds, holding your breath for four seconds, exhaling for four seconds and then holding for another four seconds before inhaling again and restarting the cycle, says breathwork coach Stuart Sandeman.

"Those seconds can be all sorts of lengths, but they must all remain the same," he explains. This equal four-step pattern is where the technique derives its name.

Stuart says box breathing is best used before you do something stressful or an event that might cause you to feel anxious, like an exam or presentation.

There's no set length of time to do it for. Some people feel the positive effects after just a few minutes; others prefer to do it for as long as 15.

Breathwork originated from traditional practices like yoga and has been used in other fields like martial arts for centuries, says Stuart.

But box breathing has become popular in modern times because it can "both focus the mind and allow us to balance our nervous system".

He adds: "Famously, the US Navy Seals are box breathers. They use it before going into a hostile situation."

Stuart has also taught breathwork to the England football team.

For Maria, 31, who works as a programme manager for a tech company in the US, she does it before she goes to bed, or when trying to get back to sleep after waking up in the night.

A recent study from North America looking at the effectiveness of box breathing found it could prevent large increases in heart rate and other stress markers in the body among people facing high-pressure situations.

The study, published in the journal Comprehensive Psychoneuroendocrinology in June, was undertaken by academics at Texas State University and the University of Toronto Mississauga.

Dr Helen Garr, a GP who treats doctors and nurses suffering mental health difficulties, says: "I recommend box breathing to lots of my patients because it is one of the most powerful evidence-based hacks that we have to take control of our stress response and our nervous system."

She says the last step of box breathing, where you hold after you exhale, is what causes the greatest change physiologically.

"What is happening inside our bodies during the final hold is that we are retaining carbon dioxide (CO2) and when our brain detects the increased levels of CO2, it feels panic. We feel that urge to breathe."

That final hold trains us to better cope with higher levels of CO2 in our system and reduce that feeling of stress, she says. People breathe differently when they're stressed, which leads to changes in their body's CO2 levels.

"Box breathing trains us to get used to variations in carbon dioxide in the blood and in the brain and helps overcome feelings of panic," she explains.

Unlike Maria, Brittany Lamm doesn't box breathe before she goes to sleep but does so after waking up.

"I do it every morning," the 28-year-old tells me from her home in California. "I actually did it just before you called me."

She found out about box breathing online a few years ago when she was going through a difficult time in her personal life and was looking for ways to cope with the stress of it.

Many people who use box breathing, from former soldiers to lifestyle influencers, share tips on how others can use it in their lives. Some also post animated guides for people to follow along with.

"If you wake up feeling anxious, it's a really great tool to help get you back into your body and out of your head," says Brittany.

It helps her feel a sense of control over her thoughts and emotions instead of letting them dictate her day.

She found it so effective that she learnt about other breathing techniques and incorporates them into her work as a life coach. She did a degree in psychology and is training to be a licensed therapist.

"I do it with my clients when we start our calls, so that they feel calmer than when they arrived.

"If we're talking about [emotionally] heavy topics, like what's going on in their relationship, it makes it a little bit easier for them."

She appreciates that some people might be sceptical about the difference breathing techniques actually make to stressful situations but urges people to try them.

"Breathwork isn't a one-size-fits-all. There's so many different types for whatever you might be feeling or going through."

She adds: "Nine out of 10 people that I work with say they really do feel so much better afterwards."

Maria feels similarly and has recommended box breathing to many friends and colleagues who have gone through stressful periods.

Fortunately for her, none of her immediate family died in the Venezuela earthquakes which are estimated to have killed at least 6,300 people.

"But my best friend lost her home and I know people who lost family and friends."

Sleepless nights still afflict Maria occasionally but box breathing is something she knows can help her deal with periods that might feel overwhelming.

"I think that sometimes we forget to breathe, like really intentionally breathe, and we underestimate the powers that it might bring to our body and mind."

articles.title: Delhi model murder: Accused Imran was booked under POCSO Act in 2018 for sexually harassing minor
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A city gym trainer accused of murdering a 21-year-old woman in west Delhi’s Tilak Nagar was injured in both legs during a police encounter .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A city gym trainer accused of murdering a 21-year-old woman in west Delhi’s Tilak Nagar was injured in both legs during a police encounter in Rajouri Garden Thursday night. He opened fire at the personnel.Muskan Sharma was murdered, allegedly by Mohammad Imran, alias Aqib, at her home Wednesday.Police said Imran resisted arrest and fired at the team, following which the personnel retaliated. Three of the seven rounds fired by the police hit him in the legs. He was rushed to hospital, where he is currently undergoing treatment.Also read: 'Imran’s drug dependence, suicide bid, hotel meeting': More skeletons tumble out in Delhi model Muskan’s murderPolice are also probing whether Imran had gone live on social media shortly before the murder and threatened Muskan that he will kill her. Sources said she had stopped taking his calls and blocked him on social media, following which he allegedly contacted her using different numbers. Investigators suspect he may have called her on the day of the murder and became enraged when she did not respond.Suspect changed locations frequentlyPolice inquiry revealed that Imran was booked under Pocso Act in 2018 for allegedly sexually harassing a minor in Tilak Nagar. The case also invoked sections related to voluntarily causing hurt, stalking, outraging modesty and common intention.Sources said it was not his first criminal case. In 2021, he was also involved in a culpable homicide case in which he allegedly assaulted a man who suffered serious head injuries and went into a coma.The complainant told police that on the night of Oct 30, 2020, Imran struck him on the head with a stone slab. While he was lying on the ground, Imran allegedly struck him on the nose with the same stone slab. He remained admitted to the hospital for six days. A case was registered next year, on court’s order.According to police, after killing Muskan, Imran allegedly took her iPhone, possibly to delete text messages and chats and prevent any digital trail from being recovered. Police said after fleeing the crime scene, Imran kept changing his location. Multiple police teams conducted raids across west Delhi and adjoining areas to trace him.DCP (West) Hareshwar Swami said Thursday evening, a police team spotted a suspicious individual near the sub-registrar’s office in Rajouri Garden.On closer inspection, the personnel identified him as Imran and tried to nab him. However, he allegedly opened fire at the team, prompting them to retaliate. Imran sustained gunshot injuries to both legs in the exchange. Eleven rounds were fired during the encounter; Imran fired four rounds while the cops fired seven, three of which hit him on his knees.As Imran remains hospitalised, investigators have not yet been able to question him about the source of the weapon and the motive behind the murder.Muskan’s family had told police she had been repeatedly harassed by Imran for a long time. Police said they also found that Imran suspected she was talking to another man, which he did not like.Police are also looking into the suspect’s Instagram account. His profile features posts about his gym workouts and cricket activities. However, a video uploaded from his account in 2019 shows a group of men sitting inside a room while music plays in the background. articles.title: Pakistani drone detected in Jammu and Kashmir's Rajouri, security forces put LoC sector on high alert
articles.summary: India News: Security forces along the Line of Control (LoC) in Jammu and Kashmir have been put on high alert after fresh aerial activity originating from across t.
articles.body: Security forces along the Line of Control (LoC) in Jammu and Kashmir have been put on high alert after fresh aerial activity originating from across the border was detected in the Poonch district.According to inputs from Army sources cited by news agency ANI, an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) from Pakistan was detected at around 8:05 pm on Friday.The drone was spotted hovering over the general area of Behrooti village in the Balakote area of Poonch's Mendhar sector, which falls under the operational area of responsibility of the 22 Jammu and Kashmir Rifles (22 JAK RIF).Drone tracked towards Mangalnar-Dabrote axisMilitary personnel tracked the UAV as it manoeuvred towards the Mangalnar-Dabrote side near the border before returning to Pakistan.Alert troops immediately logged the intrusion, following which the entire forward sector was placed under tight aerial and ground surveillance.Security forces launched the search operation at first light on Saturday in adjoining forward areas to check for any possible dropping of contraband or arms.Monitoring along the border remains active, and further official updates are awaited.Similar drone sightings reported along borderThe latest incident comes amid heightened security concerns along the India-Pakistan border and follows other suspected drone sightings reported in Jammu and Kashmir in recent weeks.Earlier this month, security forces launched a search operation after a suspected Pakistani drone was spotted over forward villages along the International Border in Jammu and Kashmir's Kathua district.The BSF and Jammu and Kashmir Police conducted searches to ensure that no weapons, explosives or other material had been dropped.A suspected Pakistani drone was also spotted in Rajouri's Sunderbani sector last month, after which security forces carried out a search operation but found nothing suspicious.Earlier in June, Army personnel opened fire after spotting a Pakistani drone over forward posts in the Balakote sector of Poonch, forcing it to retreat towards Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.Notably, the latest incident also comes days after an unusual increase in Turkish military transport flights to Pakistan raised concerns in Indian defence circles.Open-source flight trackers recorded a surge in Turkish C-130 Hercules and A400M aircraft flights between August 19 and 21, with the planes landing at Pakistani air bases, including Nur Khan, Masroor and Murid.There was speculation in defence circles that the flights may have carried military hardware, including unmanned aerial systems and air-defence equipment, although neither Pakistan nor Turkey officially confirmed the nature or cargo of the operations.Separately, security forces are carrying out massive search operations in the forested districts of Udhampur, Kathua and Rajouri following information about suspicious movement, according to news agency PTI.In Rajouri, another search operation was launched in Gaibas, Mithiyani, Mogla and Narla after villagers reported the movement of two suspected armed persons, believed to be terrorists.No contact with any suspected persons had been established so far, officials said.The latest incident in Poonch comes as security forces continue to maintain heightened surveillance along forward areas of Jammu and Kashmir.Get the latest India
